hints.junior: Pasting a symptom and getting a cure back means the reasoning in between never happened where you could learn it.
hints.mid: A diff that fixes the symptom without a hypothesis ever being formed, tested, and confirmed is a fix with no attached learning event.
hints.staff: An AI debugging assistant that defaults to instant answers is always choosing the low-transfer path — it resolves the current ticket fastest, not the next one.

hints.junior: Step through both conversations and count how many turns it takes to reach the fix in each — and notice what the user has to do to get there.
hints.mid: Broken mode resolves in one assistant turn. Fixed mode walks expected-vs-actual, then data source, then timing, before the user reaches their own conclusion.
hints.staff: Fixed mode's last turn hands the final inferential step back to the user instead of stating the root cause for them — that's deliberate, not an incomplete answer.

hints.junior: Answering guiding questions forces the same diagnostic steps a senior engineer runs silently — out loud, where you actually have to do the reasoning.
hints.mid: Each question targets a specific diagnostic move — expected-vs-actual, last-known-good, trace-the-data-source — that a fluent debugger already runs automatically.
hints.staff: Without an escalation path after 2-3 stalled questions, this just becomes an obstacle — pure withholding isn't pedagogically better than instant answers, it's differently unhelpful.

hints.junior: This is a UX decision, not a stricter system prompt — default mode, how many questions before a hint, and a visible 'just show me' escape hatch all matter.
hints.mid: The escalation ladder matters more than the first question — each rung should narrow the search space further than the last, not just rephrase the same question.
hints.staff: The hard part is generating a question that's diagnostic for this specific bug and this learner's stated understanding — a generic 'have you checked your inputs?' degrades into the same boilerplate the case warns against.

sections.junior: Today's case is about a developer who pasted a stack trace into an AI chat, got a working fix back in ten seconds, and then couldn't recognize the exact same bug two weeks later, because they never actually diagnosed it the first time.
sections.mid: Instant-answer debugging optimizes time to green at the expense of whether anyone actually built a reusable mental model of the failure.
sections.staff: This is the assistant version of a known problem in learning research — handing over a fully worked solution removes the retrieval practice that produces durable, transferable understanding.

sections.junior: A Socratic debug coach asks a few guiding questions before it reveals anything. What did you expect versus what actually happened, what's the last state you know was working, where does this data actually come from.
sections.mid: Each question targets a specific diagnostic move that a fluent debugger already runs automatically, just made explicit and out loud.
sections.staff: The design needs an escalation path. If a few guided questions go nowhere, offer a more direct hint rather than stonewalling — the goal is scaffolded struggle with a floor under it, not struggle for its own sake.

sections.junior: Try clicking through both conversations and see how differently each one gets to the fix.
sections.mid: Watch how many turns each mode takes, and notice who's actually doing the reasoning at each step.
sections.staff: Pay attention to the very last turn in the guided version — it asks the user how they'd guard for the bug instead of just telling them.

sections.junior: Getting a fix handed to you in one turn feels fast, but it skips the reasoning that would let you catch the same bug next time on your own.
sections.mid: Default to guided questions before revealing a fix, and make instant answers an explicit opt-out instead of the default behavior.
sections.staff: Build a real escalation ladder with a visible escape hatch — withholding answers indefinitely is just as unhelpful as handing them over instantly, in the opposite direction.
